Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A medical-equipment visual trigger is hard to reconcile as a central combat-related trigger for this profile, especially alongside otherwise combat-consistent threat items and without any medical/hospital-related memory or appraisal content. It suggests a different trauma context and is clinically difficult to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense rage on recall conflicts with the paired reports of emotionally numb recall and the memory feeling alien/detached. Fluctuation can occur, but as a compact three-item profile these items pull in opposing directions—high emotional arousal versus marked dissociative detachment—without other memory content to bridge them.

Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Rage on Recall' conflicts with the paired endorsement of markedly detached recall ('Emotionless Recall' and 'Memory Feels Alien'). Intense rage during recall and recall experienced as numb/alien can both occur in PTSD, but selecting all three as coequal memory descriptors creates a direct within-node tension between highly affect-laden remembering and strongly depersonalized, affectless remembering. The rest of the profile coherently reflects severe combat-related PTSD, but this specific Memory combination is the main clinically questionable inconsistency.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, two items describe markedly detached/derealized recall ('emotionless', 'belongs to someone else') while another describes intensely affect-laden reliving ('same terror I felt at the time'). These can both occur across different moments in PTSD, but as the only three selected memory items they pull in opposing directions and are not a clean, internally coherent depiction of a single dominant memory style for this profile.

These two appraisals are plausible in severe PTSD, but for a 63-year-old married airline pilot they create a hard-to-explain mismatch with the rest of the profile when presented without any trauma-linked appraisal content. 'I have no future' is especially discordant for an older, still-employed patient and is not well integrated with the combat-specific trigger/threat pattern. The Negative Appraisals node is dominated by global depressive identity/future statements rather than trauma-related meanings that would plausibly connect to the very strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals edge in the formulation.

vignette:
Matiu had spent most of his adult life in the cockpit, but since returning from combat he no longer moved through the world with the easy confidence his family remembered. The event that had changed him was tied to a particular evening on deployment: the low thud of helicopters overhead, the rough, almost abrasive texture of equipment straps and a coarse seat covering under his hands, and the exact hour when the light outside had been paling toward night. In the months after, those same textures could seize him without warning. If he brushed against a similar fabric in a hotel chair or caught the wash of rotors from a passing aircraft, his body went rigid and his attention snapped to his surroundings. He would scan for exits the moment he entered a room or building, and when night fell he found it much harder to feel safe than during the day, as if the world could open into danger again at any moment. The sudden movements of other people, even a waitress turning quickly or his wife reaching across the table, put him immediately on guard.

What troubled Matiu most was that the memory of the combat did not feel like his own life. He described it as something that belonged to someone else, yet when it came it did so with full force, not as a distant recollection but with the same terror he had felt at the time. A helicopter sound over the freeway, or the feel of a rough strap against his palm, could instantly bring the whole scene back without warning, and once that happened his fear sharpened. He became more watchful, more tense, checking doors and windows, measuring movements, and bracing for threat, and that heightened vigilance made the ordinary textures and sounds around him stand out as possible signs of danger. In that state he noticed more things that reminded him of the event, which kept the memory close and emotionally vivid rather than fading.

As the replays continued, Matiu came to believe there was something wrong with him as a person. He told himself that a man who should have been able to handle what happened would not be left this fragile, this easily shaken, and he felt ashamed that he could no longer recognize himself as the happy person he used to be. In his mind the world had become a dangerous place, and that belief made every abrupt motion, every passing aircraft, every unfamiliar room feel loaded with threat. Because he saw himself as defective and the world as unsafe, he became even more alert for anything that might set him off, and he started noticing helicopter sounds or certain rough textures almost before he could think. The more he watched for danger, the more often those cues seemed to appear, and the more often they appeared, the more his conviction deepened that he was broken and that the world could not be trusted.

At home, the pattern narrowed his life. He avoided evening errands and preferred not to linger in crowded places after dark. At work, he noticed himself tensing when another aircraft passed low or when a colleague moved too quickly across the hangar, and though he had spent years managing pressure in the air, he now found himself scanning every space on the ground. His wife saw him grow distant and irritable, and he hated that he no longer felt like the man who had once been steady and cheerful. What finally brought him to seek help was the sense that the fear was no longer staying in the background; it was invading ordinary moments, stealing sleep and peace, and making him worry that he would spend the rest of his life on guard. He came wanting some relief from the terror that still rushed back so vividly, and he was most afraid that if nothing changed, he would remain trapped in this version of himself, always alert, always miserable, and unable to trust the world again.
